forces: Orchestra with piano, celesta and two harps
performers: Orchestre de la Suisse Romande; Ernest Ansermet
question: How does Stravinsky turn a change of orchestral texture into a change of scene?
intro: A St Petersburg fair contains several musics at once: the crowd, street entertainers and a puppet theatre. In the original orchestration, piano, celesta and two harps give the mechanical performers distinct attacks among the winds and strings.

sections.label: The fairground crowd
sections.mNote: flute figures over repeating clarinet and horn patterns

sections.label: Street entertainers
sections.mNote: organ-grinder and music-box episodes interrupt the crowd

sections.label: The Charlatan’s magic
sections.mNote: slow wind figures and an unaccompanied flute cadenza

sections.label: Russian Dance
sections.mNote: piano and wind attacks animate the three puppets

cues.title: Several motions at once
cues.text: The opening flute figure rides above repeating clarinet and horn patterns. Listen separately to the moving tune and the rocking accompaniment: the fair begins with simultaneous layers, not a melody waiting for its accompaniment to catch up.
cues.evidence: Score p. 7 gives flute, clarinets and horns before the solo cellos join. The cached analysis begins with active sound and a rising relative level across 0:00–0:35; this is an opening-passage description, not a timed cello entrance. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A reconstructed Petersburg fair
cues.text: The scenario sets the action at a St Petersburg Shrovetide fair around 1830. Its stalls, swings, samovar and little puppet theatre are specified stage objects, not a documentary recording of a real nineteenth-century crowd.
cues.evidence: Kirchmeyer’s catalogue, Summary, transcribes the original setting and scenery. https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka

cues.title: Crowd and individual acts
cues.text: Across this first scene, keep track of the difference between massed dance music and smaller street acts. Stravinsky can clear the orchestral foreground for an entertainer without making the surrounding fair disappear from the story.
cues.evidence: The report shows the early crest at 0:55–1:05 retreating by 1:15, before changes at 1:26, 1:40 and 1:52. The distinction between crowd and entertainers comes from the scenario, not instrument separation by the analysis. https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Room for street music
cues.text: In the street-entertainer episodes, the thick crowd texture gives way to smaller combinations. Listen for repeated little patterns that can keep going while another tune attracts attention beside them.
cues.evidence: Rehearsals 9–16 alternate the crowd, organ-grinder and music box. Boundaries at 1:40 and 1:52, followed by much lower relative levels from 2:05, place this broad sequence; no individual stage entrance is fixed here. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A mechanical accompaniment
cues.text: The organ-grinder’s music uses repeated wind figures rather than an actual barrel organ in the orchestra. The score also gives the street dancer a triangle: a simple pulse can remain audible beneath a tune with a different contour.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 21–22, rehearsals 12–13, supplies the wind patterns and triangle. The 2:05–2:45 stretch is consistently quieter than the crowd, with repeated detected attacks; placement is approximate. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two competing entertainments
cues.text: The printed stage directions put a second dancer and music box at the opposite end of the stage from the organ-grinder. The first dancer resumes her triangle while the rival act continues: competition is built into the scenario as well as the orchestration.
cues.evidence: Kirchmeyer, original-version structure, rehearsals 15–16. This describes the written scene without claiming the precise instant of either dancer’s action. https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka

cues.title: The crowd takes over
cues.text: As the broader fair music returns, the little repeating patterns give way to heavier exchanges between orchestral groups. Compare the renewed weight with the preceding street acts; the setting has stayed the same while the musical foreground changes.
cues.evidence: The report rises from −22.3 dB at 3:15 to −13.0 dB at 3:25 and reaches another broad crest at 3:50–4:00. Rehearsals 17–29 restore crowd episodes. The boundary is a passage estimate. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The seam is audible
cues.text: Listen for abrupt changes of rhythmic profile rather than a continuously developing melody. The fair’s different activities can interrupt one another; their juxtaposition is part of the form, not a transition that needs to be concealed.
cues.evidence: The report marks a change at 4:20, between the 3:50–4:00 crest and the later build. The score alternates crowd and barker episodes in rehearsals 18–29; this note names the method, not an exact entrance. https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Gathering the crowd’s attention
cues.text: This later fairground stretch accumulates orchestral weight before the puppet theatre takes over. Follow the rising pressure across the whole passage; the eventual reduction of forces matters as much as the crest.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/stravinsky-petrushka-fair.txt: relative level rises across 4:35–5:10, with 5:10 the strongest five-second window. The score’s theatrical sequence is separately documented at https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka; the report alone does not identify the drummers.

cues.title: A different scale of motion
cues.text: The Charlatan’s scene replaces the fair’s bustle with slow, separated gestures. Low wind colours and delicate keyboard and harp writing prepare the flute’s spell: orchestral space now belongs to a single theatrical act.
cues.evidence: Score p. 41, rehearsal 30, is Lento, with bassoons, contrabassoon, clarinets, horns, celesta, harp and muted strings. The report’s 5:18 boundary leads to greatly reduced brightness at 5:20–5:45; this supports passage placement, not every part’s first note. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The magician’s flute
cues.text: In the magic-trick sequence, a solo flute cadenza represents the Charlatan playing his instrument. The written accompaniment falls silent for the cadenza; its freedom of pacing contrasts with the fair’s repeating mechanisms.
cues.evidence: Score p. 41, rehearsal 31: flute cadenza, “ad lib. ma non accel.” The 5:52 change and quiet, low-brightness stretch at 5:55–6:10 support this approximate placement. No individual flute note has been aligned. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Debussy hears the magic
cues.text: Writing to Stravinsky on 13 April 1912, Debussy singled out the magic-trick music and its transformation of mechanical beings into human ones. His letter treats orchestration as part of the drama, not merely as decoration.
cues.evidence: IRCAM reproduces the dated Debussy letter, including its discussion of “le tour de passe-passe”. Paraphrased here, not a new translation presented as a quotation. https://resources.ircam.fr/en/work/petrouchka

cues.title: The puppets dance together
cues.text: The Russian Dance brings a sharply articulated collective pulse after the magic scene’s freer gestures. Piano chords and wind attacks help give the three puppets their public, apparently coordinated movement.
cues.evidence: Score p. 44, rehearsal 33, begins Allegro giusto with piano, winds, horns, cornets and pizzicato strings. Relative level rises sharply between 7:10 and 7:20 and attack density increases. The estimate locates the passage, not its first bar. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Piano inside the orchestra
cues.text: Through the dance, follow the piano as an orchestral instrument. Its sharply defined attacks can reinforce the winds rather than behaving like a concerto soloist standing apart from them.
cues.evidence: The Russian Dance score, pp. 44–61, assigns the piano both chordal and running material. The analysis rises again at 7:40–7:55; it does not isolate the pianist. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Before it was a ballet
cues.text: Stravinsky first imagined a concert work in which a puppet-like piano provoked an answering orchestra. Diaghilev heard the new music in Switzerland and persuaded him to make the puppet’s suffering the subject of a ballet.
cues.evidence: IRCAM quotes Stravinsky’s account of the Konzertstück and Diaghilev’s visit. The recollection is attributed to the composer, not treated as a session document. https://resources.ircam.fr/en/work/petrouchka

cues.title: Space inside the dance
cues.text: The dance does not stay at one level of intensity. A quieter stretch opens space before renewed attacks bring back its public display; keep the underlying motion in mind through the withdrawal.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/stravinsky-petrushka-fair.txt: boundaries at 8:50 and 8:54 accompany low relative levels at 8:50–9:00, followed by a rise at 9:05–9:10. The score’s Russian Dance occupies pp. 44–61: https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf. No precise return bar is claimed.

cues.title: From display to confinement
cues.text: The first tableau ends the puppets’ public dance; the next takes us inside Petrushka’s room. Retain the difference between their coordinated stage act and the isolated character whose music follows.
cues.evidence: The report shows renewed energy at 9:30–9:40 and withdrawal by the 591.3-second file endpoint. The score’s curtain and next tableau are on pp. 62–63. The digital track boundary is not asserted to be an original recording splice. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

transitions.title: The crowd makes room for an entertainer
transitions.how: The score repeatedly interrupts the crowd’s wind-and-string bustle with the organ-grinder’s smaller pattern. The tempo relaxes into Meno mosso, and the reduced wind texture allows the accompaniment to sound mechanical. This is a staged interruption rather than a harmonic bridge smoothing one tune into another; the barker and crowd can reappear between the entertainer’s statements.
transitions.evidence: Rehearsals 9–12 give the alternation and tempo changes. The 1:40 boundary coincides with a relative-level and brightness drop; the 1:52 rebound warns against treating this as an uninterrupted solo episode. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf

transitions.title: Small mechanisms yield to massed motion
transitions.how: The organ-grinder and music box cease their contest, and the barker resumes his address. Stravinsky restores the earlier alternation of crowd music and declamatory gestures, enlarging the instrumental groups instead of developing the music-box pattern into a new theme. Returning rhythmic profiles make the change of foreground recognisable.
transitions.evidence: The score’s rehearsals 17–18 restore the barker and crowd. Relative level rises at 3:20–3:25 after the quieter 2:05–3:15 interval. The section boundary is estimated from that contour. https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka

transitions.title: Percussion clears the stage for the spell
transitions.how: The crowd’s crescendo is diverted into the theatre drummers’ repeated strokes. Most orchestral parts then fall away, and Lento introduces low wind figures with celesta, harp and muted strings. The change separates the public fair from the Charlatan’s controlled demonstration; the later flute cadenza suspends the regular pulse further.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 39–41, rehearsals 28–31. The report marks 5:06, 5:12 and 5:18, with brightness falling from 3591 Hz at 5:00 to 467 Hz at 5:20. These locate the broad interruption, not the first drumstroke. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf

transitions.title: Free gesture becomes a collective beat
transitions.how: The magic sequence ends with flute gestures and harp glissandi, then the Russian Dance establishes Allegro giusto. Piano chords, wind attacks and pizzicato strings make the new pulse explicit. The puppets are animated together: the join is a change from flexible solo display to coordinated rhythm, not a gradual acceleration through the cadenza.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 43–44, end of rehearsal 32 into 33. The report moves from low level at 7:05–7:10 to a pronounced rise by 7:20, with more detected attacks. The 432-second estimate is provisional. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf

source.title: Stravinsky, Petrushka, 1911 orchestration; Édition Russe plate R.M.V. 127, Dover reprint

composer.born: 17 June 1882, Oranienbaum, near St Petersburg, Russia
composer.epithet: A composer of ballets who made the placement of an accent as consequential as a change of harmony.
facts: Russia · Switzerland 1914–20 · France 1920–39 · United States from 1939
Sergei Diaghilev · Vaslav Nijinsky · C. F. Ramuz · George Balanchine · W. H. Auden
Ballets, operas, symphonies, sacred choral music and chamber works; three successive approaches to tonality
composer.background:
Igor Stravinsky grew up in a St Petersburg household in which opera was a profession: his father, Fyodor, was a bass at the Mariinsky Theatre. Born at the family’s summer residence in Oranienbaum in 1882, Igor began piano lessons at ten but entered St Petersburg University to study law. Through a fellow student, Vladimir Rimsky-Korsakov, he met Vladimir’s father, whose private teaching became more important than a conservatory course. Regular lessons between 1905 and 1908 covered orchestration as practical work: distributing a passage among instruments, then comparing the result with the teacher’s solution. The Symphony in E♭, Scherzo fantastique and Fireworks belong to this apprenticeship, with traces of Tchaikovsky, Alexander Glazunov and the Russian fairy-tale orchestra.

In 1906 he married his cousin Catherine Nossenko; their four children were born between 1907 and 1914. Sergei Diaghilev heard the young composer’s orchestral music in 1909 and first employed him to orchestrate Chopin for Les Sylphides. A larger commission followed: The Firebird, with choreography by Michel Fokine. Its premiere at the Paris Opéra on 25 June 1910, with Tamara Karsavina in the title role, made Stravinsky’s reputation outside Russia. The distinction between human and supernatural characters is audible in the harmony: folk-like diatonic tunes for Ivan and the princesses, chromatic and symmetrical scales for the Firebird and Kashchei. The closing horn melody expands into an orchestral procession without abandoning its short repeating phrases.
